desc:
A string of digits is additive if it can be cut into at least three non-empty pieces that are non-negative integers with these properties:

  • no piece has a leading zero (a piece equal to 0 is written as a single 0);
  • starting from the third piece, every piece equals the sum of the two pieces before it.

Return true if num is additive. Example: "112358" is additive (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8). "199100199" is additive (1, 99, 100, 199). "1023" is not: the only way to start with 1 and 0 would need the next piece to be 1, but it is 23, and a piece such as 02 is forbidden.

The pieces can be larger than 32-bit integers; the string has at most 35 digits.
hints: Once the first two pieces are fixed, all later pieces are forced. So the search is only over the first two pieces.
Try every length for the first piece and every length for the second one. Reject a piece with a leading zero and more than one digit.

After fixing the first two numbers, repeatedly compute their sum as a string and check that num continues with it at the current position. Succeed if you reach the end of the string with at least three pieces.
editorial: Choose the first piece num[0:i] and the second piece num[i:j]; there are O(n2) such choices and each one fixes the whole sequence. Python integers do not overflow, but in other languages the pieces can be added as digit strings.

For each choice, simulate: compute x + y, write it as text and check that it matches num at the current position, then slide the two operands forward. Because j < n there is always at least one more piece to match, so a successful run has three or more pieces. Break out of a loop as soon as a piece would start with a leading zero, because every longer piece with the same start is invalid too. Total cost is O(n3) in the worst case, which is tiny for n ≤ 35.
